notes:
After working through the available sources, here are verse-by-verse notes on Hosea 5. I reached the search and fetch limits partway through, so some traditions and perspectives (Lutheran, Methodist, modern scholarship, Catholic/Orthodox) could not be fully explored. Where I could not find material, I have noted that.

---

# Hosea 5 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is commonly understood as **God's "verdict"** (the second section of the judgment cycle in Hosea 4:1–5:14). God addresses the priests, the people, and the royal house — holding the leaders especially responsible for entrapping the nation in idolatry. Judah, which had seemed slightly better in chapter 4, is now named alongside Israel as sharing in the guilt and coming punishment. The chapter closes with God's withdrawal and a note of future hope: "in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me."

- **Precept Austin** (Ryrie Study Bible outline): "2. The verdict, Hosea 5:1–15." Robert Chisholm notes five "Judgment-Salvation" cycles in Hosea; the third cycle runs Hosea 4:1–5:14 (judgment) and 5:15–6:3 (salvation).  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

- **Gill**: "The design of this chapter is to expose the sins of Israel and of Judah, and to declare the judgment of God upon them for them… and yet the chapter concludes with a promise of the conversion of these people."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **Ellicott**: The prophet addresses the priests and royal house "at the commencement of the reign of Pekah." Judah's inclusion suggests this oracle came later than Hosea 4, since Judah's defection was now more apparent (cf. Hosea 4:15).  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

---

## Verse 1 — Summons to the Leaders

> *"Hear this, O priests! Take heed, O house of Israel! Give ear, O royal house! For this judgment is against you because you have been a snare at Mizpah, a net spread out on Tabor."*

- **Three groups addressed.** The priests (spiritual leaders), the house of Israel (the people/nation), and the royal house (political leaders). Three Hebrew imperatives match the three groups: *shama* ("hear and obey"), *qashab* ("pay close attention"), and *azan* ("give ear"). Precept Austin: "All society is addressed, beginning with the priests, including the Israelites and finally the leaders (kings)."  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

- **Leaders are the primary culprits.** Enduring Word (Guzik): "It would be tempting for the priests to blame the people, but it was really the fault of the spiritual leadership (priests) and political leadership (house of Israel)."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **Snare at Mizpah, net on Tabor.** The leaders are pictured as hunters trapping prey. Ellicott locates Mizpah east of the Jordan (in Gilead) and Tabor on the west side — both military strongholds "where the princes of the royal house, with the apostate priests, exercised their deadly hold upon the people, waylaying them, as birds and beasts are snared." Gill adds that Jeroboam set up idol-altars on these high places, entrapping not only the northern tribes but also drawing in people from Judah and Benjamin.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- Precept Austin notes the tragic irony: Mizpah was where Samuel once summoned Israel for covenant renewal (1 Sam 7), and Tabor was the site of Deborah and Barak's victory (Judg 4). "The very places that should have reminded Israel of God's faithfulness instead became instruments of apostasy."  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

---

## Verse 2 — Deep in Slaughter

> *"The rebels are deep in slaughter; but I will chastise them all."*

- **A difficult verse.** Precept Austin notes this is "one of the more difficult verses in Hosea to interpret." The Hebrew can be read in several ways. Ellicott, following Ewald, renders: "The apostates have gone deep in iniquity." The NET translates: "Those who revolt are knee-deep in slaughter." The KJV/ESV retains the "slaughter" language, which may continue the hunting/snare metaphor — the leaders are "butchering" the people spiritually.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

- **"I will chastise them all."** Ellicott corrects the KJV: "But I (i.e., Jehovah) am chastisement to them all. The deceivers and deceived shall alike perish." Gill reads it as God rebuking them through prophets and judgments, yet they refused correction. Precept Austin cites Chisholm: *musar* (chastisement) "refers here to severe punishment designed to restore one to proper behavior. As such, it is an expression of love that arises out of a close relationship (cf. Prov. 3:11; 13:24; 15:5)."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

---

## Verse 3 — God Knows Ephraim

> *"I know all about Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from Me. For now, O Ephraim, you have turned to prostitution; Israel is defiled."*

- **God's omniscience.** Gill: "Though they may cover their designs from men… yet God, who knows all men, and their hearts, cannot be deceived." Precept Austin: "God's statement, 'I know Ephraim,' is not merely an acknowledgment of His omniscience but a declaration that He knows them intimately — their outward actions, inward motives, and secret sins."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/hosea-5-commentary

- **"Turned to prostitution" / "defiled."** Both spiritual adultery (idolatry) and literal sexual immorality are in view. Gill: "both corporeal and spiritual adultery, which frequently went together, as observed in the preceding chapter."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

---

## Verse 4 — A Spirit of Prostitution

> *"Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God, for a spirit of prostitution is within them, and they do not know the LORD."*

- **Two readings of "do not permit."** The KJV/Ellicott read it as "They will not frame their doings to turn unto their God" — a matter of the will, not of external impossibility. The margin reading (favoured by some Jewish commentators) is "Their deeds will not suffer (them)" — meaning sin has created a fixed moral inability. Ellicott prefers the active reading. Gill takes it as the people's obstinate unwillingness, "they had no mind to repent of their sins."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **"Spirit of prostitution."** An inner, dominating impulse toward idolatry. Gill calls it "an unclean spirit, that prompts them to and pushes them on to commit corporeal and spiritual whoredom." Ellicott: "The knowledge of the only true God is life."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **Enduring Word (Guzik)** draws an application: "When people think they're searching for God through various churches or paths, they may actually be running away — backing off whenever God starts to get close to them."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** notes that God "requires of sinners a willingness to 'frame their doings to turn unto their God.' We must gladly allow the Holy Spirit to regenerate and purify our souls."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/5.htm

---

## Verse 5 — Pride and Stumbling

> *"Israel's arrogance testifies against them; Israel and Ephraim stumble in their iniquity; even Judah stumbles with them."*

- **Pride as evidence.** Ellicott takes "the pride of Israel" to mean the false objects of their pride — their idolatrous pomp — rather than Jehovah (though some take it as Jehovah Himself being the true "pride of Israel" who testifies against them). Ellicott: "Arrogance led Ephraim… to resent the supremacy of Judah. This jealousy culminated in the rebellion of Jeroboam I."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- **Judah now included.** This is a new development from chapter 4, where Judah was warned separately (Hos 4:15). Gill: "Judah also shall fall with them… though not at the same time; for the Babylonish captivity, in which Judah was carried captive, was many years after." Enduring Word: "While Judah may have been better than Israel, they still had to repent."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

---

## Verse 6 — Superficial Seeking

> *"They go with their flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but they do not find Him; He has withdrawn Himself from them."*

- **Costly but empty worship.** Ellicott: "The vain effort to repent when it is too late. The spirit with which sacrifices of flocks and herds were offered is of more consequence than the multitude of such oblations (Micah 3:4; Isaiah 1:11; Psalm 40:6)."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- **God has withdrawn.** Gill: "The glory of the Lord departed from them; his Shechinah, or divine Majesty, as the Targum, removed from them." Enduring Word: "We can be so set in our sin and rebellion that God just leaves us to ourselves. Usually we don't even notice at first."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** The people "endeavored to pacify the Divine anger by bringing costly sacrifices of flocks and herds. But, although the people sought the Lord thus, they did 'not find him;' for they came in a spirit of slavish fear, and did not bring the sacrifice of a contrite heart."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/5.htm

---

## Verse 7 — Illegitimate Children and the Devouring New Moon

> *"They have been unfaithful to the LORD; for they have borne illegitimate children. Now the New Moon will devour them along with their land."*

- **"Strange/illegitimate children."** Ellicott: offspring that followed in the ways of their idolatrous mother, with reference to intermarriage with heathens. Gill: children "educated by them in an idolatrous way… alienated from him and his worship."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **"New Moon will devour them."** Several interpretations exist:
  - Ellicott: the "month" may personify the period during which the invasion by Tiglath-pileser takes place (2 Kings 15:29).
  - Gill reports the Jewish view that it refers literally to the month Ab (when Jerusalem was destroyed) or Tammuz; he also notes the view that the new moon festival — supposed to be a time of worship — would ironically become the occasion of their destruction.
  - The Pulpit Commentary: "A month shall devour them," i.e., destruction shall come as swiftly as the moon wanes.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/hosea/5.htm

---

## Verse 8 — The Alarm Sounded

> *"Blow the ram's horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah; raise the battle cry in Beth-aven: Lead on, O Benjamin!"*

- **Alarm of war.** Gill: "As an alarm of war, to give notice that the enemy is at hand, just ready to invade." Ellicott distinguishes the *cornet* (curved animal horn) from the *trumpet* (straight metallic instrument for convoking the congregation, Num 10:2). Gibeah and Ramah were lofty hills on the northern boundary of Benjamin — watchtowers visible from Jerusalem. Ellicott: "Hosea does not mention the metropolis, but he reveals the imminent peril of Jerusalem if these high towers… were giving the alarm at the approach of the Assyrian king."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **"After thee, O Benjamin"** (or "Lead on, O Benjamin" BSB). Ellicott: "He (the enemy) is behind thee, O Benjamin." The tribe in which Jerusalem sat would be the first to face the oncoming judgment from the north.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- **Lange's Commentary** also sees this as the alarm of invasion racing southward through Benjamin.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/hosea-5.html

---

## Verse 9 — Desolation Certain

> *"Ephraim will be laid waste on the day of rebuke. Among the tribes of Israel I proclaim what is certain."*

- **Desolation foretold.** Gill: "The country of the ten tribes shall be laid desolate… and this was the day of the Lord's rebuke and chastisement of them." The desolation was "foretold by the prophets, and published in all the tribes of Israel, as what should certainly come to pass."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- Enduring Word: "Because God has withdrawn Himself from them, they will find no help or refuge when the Assyrian army attacks. They will be made desolate."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

---

## Verse 10 — Judah's Princes: Boundary-Movers

> *"The princes of Judah are like those who move boundary stones; I will pour out My fury upon them like water."*

- **Boundary stones.** Moving a landmark was forbidden in Deut 19:14 and cursed at Mount Ebal (Deut 27:17). Ellicott: The princes "break down the barrier between right and wrong, between truth and falsehood, between Jehovah and Baalim." Enduring Word cites Wood: "Judah's leaders… were not shifting physical property lines but spiritual lines established by God, changing the boundary between right and wrong."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **"Like water."** Gill: God's wrath would pour "in great abundance, and with such force and vehemence, as not to be stopped, but utterly destroy; like a flood of water."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- The **Restoration Commentary** adds: "It is not so much that alliances or agreements among nations, per se, are displeasing to God, but the motive which prompts them… an almost complete rejection of Him."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/hosea-5.html

---

## Verse 11 — Following Worthless Idols (Human Precept)

> *"Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, for he is determined to follow worthless idols."*

- **"Willingly walked after the commandment"** (KJV). Gill: not God's commandment but the commandment of Jeroboam — worshipping the calves at Dan and Bethel. Ellicott notes the rare Hebrew word *tsav* ("commandment"), which the LXX renders as "vanities" (reading *shav* instead). So the BSB rendering "worthless idols" aligns with the LXX tradition.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- Enduring Word: "Ephraim's sin was living by man's standards and opinions instead of God's. We can't walk by human precept unless we first reject God's precepts."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

---

## Verse 12 — Moth and Decay

> *"So I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like decay to the house of Judah."*

- **Slow, hidden destruction.** Ellicott: "Both images express concealed causes of irreparable destruction which come suddenly to view when it is too late." Gill: a moth "eats garments, penetrates into them, feeds on them privately, secretly, without any noise, and gradually and slowly consumes them; but at last utterly."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- Enduring Word pairs this with v. 14: God's judgment comes in two forms — subtle (moth, decay) and obvious (lion).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

---

## Verse 13 — Turning to Assyria and King Jareb

> *"When Ephraim saw his sickness and Judah his wound, then Ephraim turned to Assyria and sent to the great king. But he cannot cure you or heal your wound."*

- **The wrong healer.** Instead of turning to God in their distress, they sought political alliances. Ellicott: "Their adversity leads Ephraim to seek protection from their formidable foe instead of turning to the Lord."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- **"King Jareb"** (or "the great king"). Not a proper name of any known Assyrian monarch. Ellicott's Excursus A notes that Schrader identifies "Jareb" as meaning "King Combat" or "King Contention" — an appellative possibly for Tiglath-pileser. Enduring Word: "'Jareb' is not a known Assyrian's name but means 'warrior.'"  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **Spurgeon preached a full sermon** on this verse ("A Caution for Sin-Sick Souls," March 13, 1861). He used it to illustrate the sinner's tendency to look to anything other than God for healing — "the sinner's partial discovery of his lost estate; the wrong means which he takes to be cured of his evil." He urged hearers to turn to Christ, the true Physician, rather than to "self-righteousness, church-going, chapel-going, sacraments."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-caution-for-sin-sick-souls

---

## Verse 14 — The Lion

> *"For I am like a lion to Ephraim and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear them to pieces and then go away. I will carry them off where no one can rescue them."*

- **Ferocious and irresistible.** Gill: God would be "strong and mighty, terrible and fierce… yea, irresistible." Ellicott connects this to the Assyrian conquest under Tiglath-pileser and later Sargon, who carried away 27,290 people from Samaria. "I, even I" — emphasis on God's personal action, not merely permitting but actively judging.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm

- The **Restoration Commentary**: "The figure of God behaving like a lion toward Israel is to depict His ferocity and invincibility. God will be irresistible — like the king of beasts."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/hosea-5.html

---

## Verse 15 — Withdrawal and Hope

> *"Then I will return to My place until they admit their guilt and seek My face; in their affliction they will earnestly seek Me."*

- **God withdraws to heaven.** Ellicott: "Tenderness blends with judgment, and insulted love bleeds and hopes. The image of the lion is dropped. Jehovah speaks of 'His own place' — Heaven." Gill: God withdraws His "Shechinah, or divine Majesty," ceasing all manifestations of His regard "till they suffer punishment, and seek my face."  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/hosea/5.htm  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/hosea/5.htm

- **Restoration, not destruction.** Enduring Word: "This was the goal of God's judgment against Israel. The goal was not destruction, but restoration. Sadly, it is often only in our affliction that we earnestly seek the LORD."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

- **Spurgeon's sermon "The Present Crisis"** (July 13, 1879) on this verse: "If God is about to go then all is going, even hope itself is removing… There should be an eager desire to bring the King back that once more the heart may sun itself in the light of his favour." He exhorted sinners to confess sin directly to God rather than looking to "priests, or sacraments, or religiousnesses."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-present-crisis

- **Lange's Commentary**: "As the lion, without fear of being attacked, withdraws into his lair, so the Lord withdraws into heaven; none can or dare call Him to account. Until they make expiation = suffer. The suffering shall drive them to God."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/hosea-5.html

- **The Restoration Commentary** sees this as God withdrawing His Shekinah presence "to discipline them into a humble, penitent, faithful dependence upon Himself. Such action by God always has as its end His perfect love and blessing."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/hosea-5.html

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

### Reformed
- **Monergism.com** indexes Reformed sermons on Hosea 5 that emphasize "covenantal judgment" and the Lord's "judicial withdrawal in response to persistent rebellion, portraying divine judgment as both punitive and corrective." No full sermon transcripts were accessible within the search limits.  
  https://www.monergism.com/topics/sermon-manuscripts-mp3s-scripture/hosea/audio-multimedia/hosea-%E2%80%94-reformed-sermons-bible-4

### Baptist
- **Spurgeon (Baptist/Reformed Baptist)** preached on v. 13 and v. 15 (see above). His emphasis is evangelistic: the sinner's wrong turn to human remedies ("King Jareb") and the need to "acknowledge their offence and seek My face." He strongly rejects reliance on "priests, or sacraments, or religiousnesses."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-caution-for-sin-sick-souls  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-present-crisis

- **GTY.org (John MacArthur, Grace Community Church)** — A sermon referencing Hosea came up in search results, but it was on a different passage (likely Hosea 5 was mentioned in passing within a topical sermon). No verse-by-verse Hosea 5 teaching from GTY could be retrieved within the search limits.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)** is the primary Pentecostal-adjacent source found. Guzik, though broadly evangelical, serves in a Calvary Chapel context. His emphasis: God's restoration goal behind judgment, the danger of superficial seeking, and the pastoral warning against "walking by human precept."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/hosea-5/

### Methodist / Wesleyan / Holiness, Lutheran, Anglican
- **No results were returned** from seedbed.com, wesley.nnu.edu, lcms.org, or 1517.org for Hosea 5 within the search limits. These traditions could not be explored further.

### Other Views (Catholic, Orthodox, Modern Scholarship)
- **No results were returned** from newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, bibleodyssey.org, or netbible.org within the search limits.

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

| Theme | Source |
|-------|--------|
| Leaders bear the greatest guilt for entrapping the people | Gill, Ellicott, Guzik, Precept Austin |
| God's judgment has a restorative purpose (v. 15) | All sources |
| Superficial worship (flocks and herds without the heart) is rejected | Pulpit, Ellicott, Guzik |
| The "spirit of harlotry" is an inner, dominating impulse to idolatry | Gill, Ellicott, Precept Austin |
| Both subtle (moth/decay) and obvious (lion) judgment comes from God | Guzik, Gill, Ellicott |
| "King Jareb" = not a proper name but "warrior" / "King Combat" | Ellicott, Guzik |
| V. 15 is the hinge to the hope of restoration in Hosea 6:1–3 | Precept Austin (Chisholm), Lange |
